newsitem.title: CONGO: Peace moves in Brazzaville on 7th day of clashes.
newsitem.headline: Peace moves in Brazzaville on 7th day of clashes.

text.p: A seventh day of mortar fire and shooting shook the capital of the former French colony of Congo on Wednesday as the city's mayor tried to broker a truce and start talks.
Witnesses reported scores of bloated bodies littering the streets in the city centre and outlying suburbs, and shops ransacked by looters. The death toll remains unclear.

President Pascal Lissouba, who supporters have been at the heart of the fighting, accused former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso and his Cobra militias of prolonging the showdown and said his only condition for talks was "good faith".

French officials at the international airport, focus of clashes overnight and again on Wednesday morning, said that they would continue evacuation flights for foreign nationals trapped in the city by the political and ethnic clashes.

"I have proposed a ceasefire three times...manifestly this gentleman is afraid of democracy," Lissouba told Radio France International, accusing Sassou Nguesso of setting up a secret army in breach of agreements to disband all private militias.
The clashes began on June 5 after soldiers surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on militias and illegal arms ahead of a July 27 presidential election.

Brazzaville Mayor Bernard Kolelas, whose own militia were at the heart of similar fighting which killed at least 2,000 people in 1993 and early 1994, has kept out of the latest fighting and is trying to mediate.
He held talks on Tuesday with Lissouba and was preparing to hold talks with Sassou Nguesso on Wednesday.

Lissouba won a 1992 presidential election after Sassou Nguesso, president from 1979, bowed to calls for multi-party politics. Lissouba defeated Kolelas in the second round after Sassou Nguesso was knocked out in the first round.
Kolelas's Ninja militia has kept out of the fighting but three large shells landed in its Bacongo stronghold on Tuesday.

"We can see they are being deliberately directed towards Bacongo. Someone wants to drag us into the fighting. I doubt whether it is President Lissouba himself, but he doesn't control all his entourage," Kolelas's spokesman Hellot Mampouya said.

On Tuesday, French armoured cars protected convoys of civilian vehicles driven by French, Lebanese and other expatriate volunteers as they moved to different parts of the city centre to check on or collect potential evacuees.

France has sent 400 troops to reinforce the 450 already in Brazzaville, where they were dispatched in March in case foreigners needed to be evacuated from Kinshasa during the civil war that toppled Zaire's Mobutu Sese Seko.
French officials said on Tuesday more than 1,000 French citizens could still be in the Brazzaville area.
A U.S. military plane flew out 30 Americans and 24 other foreign residents although Washington said it had not yet decided whether remaining Americans needed rescue.
Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon said on Tuesday there were believed to be some 60 Americans in Brazzaville including about 15 workers at the embassy, which remained open despite the fighting.
